parsed.explanation: The combined operative regime shows no visitor-facing criminalisation, no facility bans, no documented border or screening friction, and a national custody rule placing prisoners by gender identity — a strong protective feature if detention ever occurs. Exposures are societal: a six-year rise in police-reported hate crimes (not disaggregated by gender identity, LGBT-wide survey with 90% verbal abuse), a documented rising organised anti-trans movement, and two provinces' school/healthcare rollbacks with override clauses. These rollbacks are mainly resident/student-facing; a travelling minor faces them only if enrolled or seeking local gender-related care, an uncertain exposure. National protections (2017) and provincial commissions with published policy are documented and operative. This sits in Reduced Risk: above any jurisdiction with enforced restrictions, below Low Risk because of rising hostility and unresolved anti-trans violence data.

entry_documents.exposure: No trans-specific entry, visa or border-screening rule is documented; the dossier expressly records none. National documents offer an X marker and a 2016 update pathway, though these are resident-facing climate signals.
entry_documents.protection: Absence of documented border friction plus a federal human-rights act covering gender identity.
entry_documents.interaction: Entry screening interacts with national identity-document norms; no mismatch-driven questioning documented.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: A 2022 broadcaster report alleged a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners and higher sexual-assault victimisation; the report is a single allegation, not a verified pattern.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: National rule places transgender prisoners by gender identity; a correctional-officer study (2022) found officers generally attentive to trans-prisoner safety; placement and care are litigable with counsel.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: If a visitor were detained, the identity-based placement rule governs the operative custody regime; litigation shows the rule is contested but courts/advocates engage.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Provincial school-pronoun statutes (one requiring parental consent under 16, with override clause) and health/education/sport statutes shielded from challenge in a second province — mostly resident/student-facing; a travelling minor is exposed only if enrolled or seeking local care.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Provincial human-rights codes covering gender identity/expression with published commission policy; anti-bullying statutes in most provinces.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Provincial facilities rules diverge from the protective national baseline; the override clauses limit legal challenge, weakening remedies in those provinces.

care_services.exposure: Healthcare rollbacks in one province (2024 statutes shielded by 2025 override); whether these deny visitors gender-related care is not documented. Incarcerated people over 12 months are considered for surgery — resident-facing.
care_services.protection: General healthcare access undocumented but no visitor-facing denial documented nationally; correctional study shows medical attention to trans prisoners.
care_services.interaction: A travelling trans minor needing care in a rollback province could encounter refusal; unquantified and uncertain.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: An advocacy organisation documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; hate crimes rose six consecutive years (+169% since 2018). The series is not disaggregated by gender identity, so anti-trans targeting level is unresolved.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Criminal code hate-motivation provisions expressly cover gender identity and expression since 2017 — documented recourse if targeted.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: The organised movement raises the probability and severity of street hostility; the hate-crime provisions frame police response as protective rather than hostile.

minors_guardians.exposure: One province requires parental consent before a student under 16 uses a preferred name/identity, enacted with an override clause; another province's health/education/sport statutes were shielded from challenge. Exposure for a visiting minor is indirect (enrolment or local care).
minors_guardians.protection: Anti-bullying statutes covering LGBTQ students in most provinces; national human-rights protections apply to minors too.
minors_guardians.interaction: A guardian with a trans minor faces divergent provincial regimes; the override clauses foreclose some judicial remedies locally.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: A 2022 survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents reported identity-based violence in five years, 90% verbal, 17% physical — LGBT-wide, so trans-specific prevalence is unresolved. The rising hate-crime stream (4,882 incidents in 2024) is not trans-disaggregated.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Hate-crime provisions and provincial human-rights commissions provide documented enforcement routes; police response is not documented as hostile to trans victims.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Violence severity appears mostly verbal; physical component exists; recourse machinery is documented as functioning.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Unknowns: whether other provinces' marker-change rules would be questioned for foreign documents; the trans-specific level of hate crime; whether healthcare rollbacks reach visitors; outcome of the prisoner litigation.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Provincial commissions with published policy and case law; national act and criminal code provisions in force since 2017.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Unknowns are open questions, not exposures; documented remedies were not shown failing, unlike recurring-violation patterns.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar tier. Both feature possible street/hostile incidents with functioning remedies — hate-crime provisions, commissions, litigation — and no custodial or criminal exposure for identity. Here the custody rule is more protective than 0.75-D's police-review model, but the rising organised anti-trans movement and provincial rollbacks offset that, netting a comparable or slightly higher position.

Below this anchor. 0.85-A shows broad social tolerance with only isolated rural friction and prompt institutional remedies. This dossier documents a rising hate-crime stream, an organised anti-trans movement, and two provinces with enacted rollbacks shielded by override clauses — more hostility than 0.85-A tolerates, holding the score beneath Low Risk.

Materially above. 0.55-B involves routine discretionary secondary screening with administrative exclusion and weak real-time remedies. This dossier records no border friction at all, documented anti-trans hate-crime recourse, and identity-based custody placement; the exposures here are societal rather than gatekept by officials.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime combines a protective national layer (gender identity in the human-rights act and hate-crime provisions since 2017, identity-based prison placement, X markers) with documented societal-hostility signals (rising hate-crime stream, organised anti-trans movement, LGBT-wide survey violence mostly verbal) and two provincial rollback regimes affecting schools and healthcare, hardened by override clauses. For an adult visitor, no enforced restriction touches border, documents, facilities, or custody; exposures are street-level and remedy-supported, placing this above the Elevated band. For a guardian travelling with a trans minor, the provincial school and healthcare rollbacks create a genuine but unquantified local exposure. Net: strong documented protections with unresolved anti-trans violence data and subnational divergence — high Reduced Risk, roughly 0.78.
